note: Places for future ships, stations and cities. `aboard`: true only on a ship or station, false only on the ground; left out, both. `water` only on the ground where the place has that water.

places.summary: A corridor cafe with real coffee grown three decks down, printed pastries and a wall screen of somewhere with weather.
Tables along a long window onto the stars; people come for the view and forget their tea going cold.
Tea grown on the hydroponic terraces, served in a garden of dwarf trees under full-spectrum light.
Open all cycle for crews coming off shift: noodle broth, sweet buns and a booth to sleep in if you must.
Real bread from real flour, rationed in the old days and now a point of pride, the line out the hatch at first shift.
A standing coffee kiosk at the transit junction, one barista who memorises a thousand orders.
Cushioned alcoves, slow tea and a rule against calls; the archivists drink here on their break.
A cafe on a tower roof garden with real wind, real weather and drones delivering pastries to the tables.
Long tables and a different stew every shift, everyone eating together the way the founders wanted.
A steaming noodle bar of eight stools, hand-pulled noodles and a broth the owner says is older than the ship.
A restaurant inside the growing deck, cooking whatever came ripe this week, with vines over the tables.
Food printers turning out dishes from every old Earth cuisine, cheap, quick and not quite right.
Cultured steak, grilled mushrooms and algae-crisp sides in a dim room of real wood panelling, which cost a fortune to ship.
Steamed dumplings by the basket, a family recipe from the founding crews, and a queue at every meal.
The formal dining room where officers host guests, with tablecloths, crystal and a dress code.
Curries made with spices grown in the herb rooms, the hottest dish on the deck and a prize for finishing it.
Fish raised in the aquaculture tanks, served raw or grilled at a bar looking into the tanks themselves.
A ring of hawker stalls under one roof, dozens of cooks, one seat for everyone and the din of the whole deck eating.
A grill on the restored seafront serving fish from the new reefs, the sea air a luxury people still talk about.
A deliberately old-fashioned diner of chrome stools, milkshakes and burgers, built from photographs of a lost world.
Twelve courses on a counter for eight, each dish built around one ingredient grown aboard.
A quiet lounge under a dome of stars, low lights, slow music and drinks served in heavy glass.
A crew bar near the docking ring, cheap synth-gin, old songs and a wall of patches from every ship that ever docked.
Spirits distilled from whatever the farms overproduced this cycle, served neat in a copper-walled room.
A brewery making beer from hydroponic barley, with a tap list that changes when the harvest does.
A bar in the weightless core where drinks come in bulbs and the regulars float in their own corners.
Wine from the vine deck, vintages named after the years of the journey, and a sommelier who remembers each one.
A bar on the hundredth floor with neon in the rain outside, a jazz trio and an expensive view.
A sober bar of tonics, fermented teas and mood drinks for people on early shift.
A bar of tabletop games, old card games and a league for a strategy game the ship invented itself.
A club with a floor that lights under your feet and a DJ who mixes from recordings of old Earth radio.
Live jazz in a low-ceilinged room, the band in old-style suits, and dancing after the second set.
Private karaoke pods with a song library of every language aboard and a bell for more drinks.
A ballroom where the old dances are taught on Tuesdays and danced on Saturdays, under a chandelier of glass bulbs.
A strip of bars and clubs under holographic signs, loud till dawn and full of people from out of system.
A theatre where actors play among holographic sets, from old Shakespeare to plays written aboard last year.
Tiered seats round a stage in the commons, used for concerts, debates and the yearly founders' pageant.
A concert hall tuned perfectly for an orchestra that plays on instruments made aboard.
Old Earth films from the archive on a big screen, with talks afterwards about what a 'sunset' was like.
Full-sense immersive rooms for an hour of forests, oceans or the surface of Mars.
Stand-up comedy in a converted cargo hold, mostly jokes about the food and the people who run the ship.
An arena for drone races, gravity-ball and concerts for the whole population at once.
The founders' museum: the first seed vault, the launch logs and a room of objects people brought from Earth.
Paintings, photographs and recordings of Earth's places, with a room that plays rain sounds for the homesick.
Hands-on exhibits about the ship's engines, the stars ahead and how the air gets made.
A domed room showing where the ship has been and where it is going, with the destination star lit gold.
The first landing pods, the first harvest and the names of everyone who made the city from bare ground.
Every book from Earth on file and a few hundred on real paper, kept behind glass and lent out by appointment.
Study pods, tutors on call and a wall of plants that keeps the air fresh during exams.
A forest under a high dome, with paths, a stream and a single old oak brought as an acorn from Earth.
Grass you are allowed to lie on, a playground and benches under sun lamps that dim at ship's evening.
A park that curves up and out of sight along the ring, so you can always see the far side above you.
A park built across the tops of three towers, with bridges between them and wind turbines like trees.
Old flooded ground restored to marsh, with boardwalks, birds and signs about what used to be here.
A quiet garden where the names of everyone lost on the journey are carved on stones among the moss.
Tiered hydroponic beds of lettuces, herbs and strawberries, with visitors allowed one berry each.
Dwarf apple, plum and lemon trees in rows, blossoming on a calendar set by the agriculture council.
A bay of flowers grown only for beauty, which caused a famous argument at council and won.
A garden that grows a little of every crop in the seed vault each year, to keep the seeds alive.
A farm forty floors high, with a public walkway up through the tomato vines to a cafe on top.
Required exercise hours for bone health, made bearable with music, climbing walls and a good pool.
A court in the weightless core for zero-g ball, flying lessons and very undignified beginners.
A long swimming pool of reclaimed water, warm baths after and a sauna that steams on the hour.
A track all the way round the ring, so you run for an hour and never reach the end.
Martial arts in a quiet room of wooden floors, the old forms taught exactly as they were on Earth.
Yoga under a skylight of stars, gentle classes for long-voyage bodies and a teacher who was born aboard.
A climbing wall up the inside of a tower, routes graded by the ship's best and a rope you will need.
Stalls of traded goods from every port of call: fabrics, spices, spare parts and things nobody can identify.
Where everybody collects their weekly provisions, the most reliable place aboard to catch up on news.
Growers selling the extra from their allotment plots: odd tomatoes, too much mint and the first peas of the cycle.
Stalls lit with paper lanterns for the night cycle: grilled skewers, cheap jewellery and fortune-telling by star chart.
A weekly barter meet where nothing is sold, only swapped, and the best trades become legends.
Fish, kelp and shellfish from the restored sea farms, sold straight from the boats each morning.
A two-level promenade of shops, from tailors to tech repair, under a ceiling painted like a summer sky.
A repair shop that fixes anything, because aboard nothing gets thrown away, and the owner is proud of it.
A tailor who makes clothes from reclaimed fabric, with a waiting list and a strict sense of style.
Handmade paper books, journals and letters, the most expensive luxury aboard and the most loved.
Souvenirs and oddities from every station the ship has visited, labelled in the owner's careful hand.
A vertical mall of a hundred shops, glass lifts and a food court with a view of the spaceport.
The biggest window aboard, where people gather to watch planets go by and children press their faces to the glass.
A wave pool with warm sand, a painted horizon and a sun lamp hot enough to burn, if you forget.
A gallery where crowds watch shuttles lift off into the sky, with a cafe and a launch timetable.
A small zoo of Earth animals bred aboard: goats, rabbits, chickens, a pair of very spoiled otters.
The aquaculture tanks opened to visitors, with jellyfish lit blue and fish that have never seen an ocean.
A gallery overlooking the bridge, where visitors can watch the ship being flown, quietly.
Bronze figures of the founding crews, their names on the base and fresh flowers left every week.
A thick window looking down into the drive core's glow, the deep hum felt through your feet.
The great lift shaft through the middle of the ship, its lights moving up and down like a heartbeat.
The base of the space elevator, a ribbon rising out of sight into the sky, with climbers going up every hour.
A tower city of a hundred floors with gardens on every tenth, the tallest building on the planet.
The great sea wall built in the bad years, with a promenade on top and the old drowned town visible at low tide.
Shuttle berths and cargo locks round the docking ring, busy with crews coming and going on shore leave.
A shuttle bay of small craft, mechanics in grease-stained coveralls and a viewing window for visitors.
The spaceport's terminals, landing pads and cargo yards, with ships to orbit leaving every few minutes.
A seaport of automated freighters and sailing yachts, with a fish quay that still runs on people.
A chapel shared by every faith aboard, its altar turned for each service and a candle that is never out.
A dark round room with a single window onto the stars, for anyone who needs to sit with something.
A temple in a garden of raked gravel and bonsai, with a bell rung at the change of each shift.
Printers, lathes and laser cutters free to use, full of people making spare parts and presents.
A luthier making violins and guitars from grown wood, each one tested by the ship's best player.
A lab where students build maintenance drones, with a public demo every week that usually goes wrong.
A pottery studio with an electric kiln, wheels for hire and a shelf of cups everyone has made at least once.
A walk end to end along the ship's spine, past every deck and window, done once by everyone on their birthday.
A trail through the arboretum's forest, with a stream to step over and a bench by the old oak.
A trail up out of the city to the ridge over the terraformed valley, the new forest spreading year by year.
A path along the city's canals, with water taxis gliding past and gardens on the old flood walls.
A beach on the restored coast, the sand brought in by barge, with swimming nets and sun shelters.
A stadium of fifty thousand for gravity-ball and the old Earth sports, with seats that heat and cool.
The clinic for every animal aboard, from farm goats to someone's very old cat, with the vet on call all cycle.
Cocoa grown on the warm deck, whipped thick and sold through a hatch to queues of children after school.
A cafe where the ship's cats live, sleep on the cushions and accept tribute in the form of attention.
Pies of mushroom, cultured beef and whatever the farms grew too much of, eaten standing at the counter.
Tacos on fresh corn tortillas from the maize terraces, salsa from the chilli room and a line every lunch.
A pub built to look like an English one from an old photograph, with a fake fireplace and real ale.
Cocktails made with lab precision and herbs from the gardens, by a bartender with a chemistry degree.
A puppet theatre that tells the founding story every week, to the delight of children and the founders' grandchildren.
Eight bowling lanes, glow-in-the-dark balls and a league that takes its rivalries very seriously.
Stalls of second-hand gadgets, old screens and spare chips, and a tinkerer who will rebuild anything.
Potted plants for cabins and flats, bred to thrive under artificial light, and advice on keeping them alive.
Themed escape rooms built from old hull sections: a reactor scare, a derelict ship and a mystery in the archive.
A mirrored studio of dance classes from ballet to old Earth line dancing, packed at the end of shift.
Glassblowers turning recycled glass into cups, lamps and the little stars people hang in their windows.
